Analysis by Richard Cowan 

I am back from helping lead the NORML Sensible Amsterdam Tour for CSTravel, and as the saying goes, a good time was had by all, but in Amsterdam that is easy. 

The coffee shops we visited were happy to show the guests their selection, which most of them sampled. (Some of the spouses of guests who were medical patients did not partake.) 

We also visited the Cannabis College, and the guests were delighted to see the small indoor garden that the college is allowed to keep. The CC is a non-profit organization in an old canal house in the “Red Light District.” It is run by a volunteer staff that was both informative and passionately committed to educating people about cannabis.

 

For me, the most informative part of the trip was a panel – which I moderated – with Sergeant Ron Beekmeijer, a 20 year veteran of the Amsterdam police department and Michael Veling, who owns the 420 Café and is also the spokesman for the Amsterdam Coffee Shop Owners Association. He is politically active in the center/right Christian Democratic Party that leads the current government, and is a very interesting fellow. 

Sergeant Beekmeijer is also in charge of the Red Light District and of coffee shop enforcement throughout the city. 

He and Veling explained how the system really works. 

First, the possession and sale of cannabis are still illegal in The Netherlands. However, under the international treaties banning cannabis, countries actually have a great deal of leeway, and the Dutch have chosen not to enforce these laws – under certain circumstances.

See 

Swiss Government Says Going Dutch Does NOT Violate Treaties. Implications for Other Countries, Especially Canada and UK. Plus Full Text of UN Nark Press Release. 

The present regulations limit personal possession to 30 grams. Individual sales are limited to 5 grams per customer, and the shops are permitted to have an inventory of no more than 500 grams That is a problem for those that carry a large variety and do a lot of business. Restocking becomes a delicate balancing act. Consequently, there is some discussion of allowing a larger inventory. 

Sergeant Beekmeijer is in favor of the complete legalization of cannabis, and would at least like to see some arrangement for regulating the supply side (“the backdoor”), but he thinks that it is not yet possible politically.

The present coalition government is somewhat “prohibitionist” in the Dutch context, and it is certainly not going to go out of its way to push the envelope. In previous parliaments there have been majorities in favor of regulating the supply, but even then the government chose not to act. 

See 

Busy, Often Bizarre Time In the World of Cannabis Prohibition. Still Bonkers In Britain. RCMP Still Lying In Canada. Dutch Parliament May Force “Legalization.” 

and 

Good News From Holland Is Even Better in Context. “Large Majority” of Dutch Parliament Favors Legalization of Cannabis. Most EU Countries Recognize Dutch Model Superior to DEAland’s. We Are Winning! 

Mark Twain once quipped, “The reports of my death have been greatly exaggerated.” I am once again happy to report that the same is true about the death of the Dutch “coffee shop system.”

 

Over the years that I have been doing MarijuanaNews.com I have run a number of articles that contradicted various reports that the Dutch were finally bowing to foreign pressure, but even those who do not like the present system know that it works better than any of the alternatives. 

One of the recurring claims that concerned Americans was that the coffee shops were to be closed to foreigners. The Germans and the Belgians complain that their citizens are crossing the open Dutch border and buying cannabis. The heavy traffic in some of the border towns is also a problem for the locals, so some of them have put the shops on the edge of the city. 

See 

Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report for May 24, 2005 Dutch NOT Closing Shops To Foreigners. Benefit of Sativex: Quacks Can’t Ignore Cannabis. Philippines Replace Cannabis with Tobacco. 

and from 2002,

see 

Dutch Government Reconfirms Coffee Shop Policy. Drops Any Mention of Closing Border Shops. The Justice Minister Is Educating the Prime Minister. 

For historical reasons, and because Amsterdam has always gone its own way, the cities have a great deal of control over the enforcement of whatever the national government decides is policy. 

See 

Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report for April 28, 2005 Dutch Mayors And People Favor Legalization. Czar’s Helper Lies To Jamaicans. Alaska Governor Dumps Public Defender. ACLU Sues DEA. 

Recently, there have been a number of stories saying that Amsterdam is becoming “less tolerant” and is cracking down on prostitution – by closing the "windows" in the Red Light District and closing coffee shops as well. 

For example, on January 7th, the Los Angeles Times carried a story, Visiting Amsterdam: Sex, drugs and second thoughts by Geraldine Baum. 

Baum devotes an odd amount of her article to a spokesman for the religious right “Christian” Union Party. As a Christian, I cannot tell you what I think of these people, but – happily – they represent only a very small minority of the Dutch people. She and the CUP equate cannabis and prostitution, and seem to approve of what they see as moves against both – for “moral” reasons. 

In fact, what is really happening is just what Americans call “gentrification.” The owner of about one third of the windows was bought out for $35 million! There is also some genuine concern about organized crime and the exploitation of women, but Amsterdam is not about to drive the women onto the streets. 

Similarly, some of the seedier coffee shops are being pressured to move or close. The Amsterdam mayor Job Cohen has made it clear that he is not going to wreck the tourism business and create a street trade for cannabis by closing too many coffee shops. 

In 2006, a few dozen of the older coffee shops that also had bars were finally forced to choose between selling alcohol and selling cannabis. It is significant that only a few chose to give up selling cannabis. (A few of the largest, like the big Bulldog and the Grasshopper, sell alcohol in one part and cannabis in another area.) 

This long anticipated move spurred a typically Dutch development. A number of coffee shop owners have started their own bar/restaurants nearby. In fact, the panel was at Barneys Uptown, a really beautiful new bar/restaurant started by Derry, the owner of Barney’s (formerly “Barneys Breakfast Bar", which is just across the street.) 

Many even have signs in their windows indicating that you can smoke your joint while you eat and drink. During the time when coffee shops could also be bars there were very few problems like those found in regular bars, and the same will be true of the bars that allow cannabis smoking. Nonetheless, it would seem that ending the bar/coffee shop combination was a solution for a non-existent problem. (Governments specialize in that.)

 

It is also true that smoking cannabis will be allowed after the ban on tobacco smoking in public places goes into effect next July. 

One of the best indications of the future of the coffee shops system can be seen in the number of nice new coffee shops being opened on Haarlemmerstraat near Barneys, in part because of Derry’s success on a street that was somewhat underserved in an improving neighborhood. The new Greenhouse there shows Arjan’s flair for design with a tank with Koi under the glass floor. 

Finally, we got more insight into Dutch policies with visit a small but beautiful “Smart Shop”, When Nature Calls (Great photo) that sells fresh mushrooms (dried mushrooms have been banned for some time), and other mild psychedelics, like Salvia. The owner, Patrick, was very informative.

It was widely reported that the sale of fresh mushrooms was also to be banned after a mentally unstable French woman got drunk, took a lot of other drugs and then ate some mushrooms and jumped into a canal. (Of course, a prohibitionist politician and the sensationalist press blamed the mushrooms!) 

However, in Amsterdam cooler heads prevailed – helped perhaps by a large demonstration against the ban. Instead of banning them, Amsterdam is requiring that they be sold with proper educational material, which includes a prominent warning against using them with alcohol. Real drug education! 

Anti-Dutch propaganda remains a staple of the prohibitionist party line, but the Dutch are not going to abandon what works for something that they know does not work. 

See 

Dutch Lessons: Tolerance Works. Prohibition Is Counterproductive. Who Is The Real Threat To Our Freedom and Security? 

and
